job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# Drafting Problems in S. 2817 (as amended October 6, 2026)

**Highest priority for Thursday:**

- **Item 1** is an internal contradiction about whether the prohibition is permanent or lasts ten years.
- **Items 4–5** (the environmental-assessment exemption and the grandfather clause) are the broadest carve-outs.
- **Items 13–14** (no penalty for failing to register, and a thin reporting duty) mean the registry provisions have little practical force.

I'm not a lawyer, and some of these points depend on doctrine that Legislative Counsel or our outside counsel should confirm before they go into talking points. Statutory references are for orientation and should be checked.

**Sections 2–3: Scope and definitions**

1. **Sec. 7(a) vs. Sec. 7(b).** Section 7(a) keeps the prohibition in place until Congress passes a joint resolution, but Section 7(b) ends the entire Act after ten years regardless. Read together, the prohibition may lapse in ten years even without a finding, which is a major gap that the sponsors would need to resolve.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A), per-vessel threshold.** The 10,000-ton trigger applies to "a single vessel," so operators could divide production across several vessels, or across affiliated companies, that each stay under the line.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A), tonnage measurement.** The bill does not say whether tonnage is wet or dry weight, whether it counts nodules brought up or nodules actually processed, or how the "per year" period is measured. Each choice moves a given operation above or below the threshold.

4. **Sec. 3(c), environmental-assessment exemption.** The exemption depends only on the activity's "purpose," with no definition of "environmental assessment," no volume cap, no approval requirement, and no restriction on selling recovered material. This is the broadest gap in the bill: commercial-scale recovery could be labeled as testing.

5. **Sec. 3(b), grandfather clause.** The clause covers "mining conducted under an exploration license issued before" enactment, but it has no volume cap, no expiration, and no bar on renewals or transfers. Exploration licenses are also not mining licenses, so the clause could be read to permit commercial extraction under an exploration instrument.

6. **Sec. 3(b), anti-rush gap.** The clause has no cutoff date tied to introduction, so licenses issued between introduction and enactment would count as grandfathered. Opponents will likely raise this, and it is a reason to expect pressure for an amendment.

7. **Sec. 3(b), terminology mismatch.** The Act does not define "exploration license" or connect it to the existing licensing regime under the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act of 1980 (DSHMRA), which uses different instrument types, including commercial recovery permits. A reading that the grandfather clause reaches DSHMRA authorizations would be a strong argument for continuity.

8. **Sec. 2(1)(B), "comparable risk" determination.** The Secretary can extend coverage to any activity the Secretary "determines" is comparably risky, but the Act sets no standard, procedure, notice requirement, or record. Because this is discretionary and unreviewable on its face, it is an opening for an APA arbitrary-and-capricious challenge in either direction.

9. **Sec. 2 (generally), "Secretary" is undefined.** The bill never identifies which Secretary (Commerce, Interior, or another official) administers the Act, which leaves the 1(B) determination and Section 6 without a clear responsible official.

10. **Sec. 2(1), "commercial" is defined by volume, not commercial character.** Activities below 10,000 tons per year on one vessel fall outside "commercial deep seabed mining" even if the material is sold. Any sales-based or profit-based concept is absent.

11. **Sec. 2(2), "U.S. person" definition.** The definition covers only natural persons and corporations organized under a State's law. It excludes LLCs, partnerships, and trusts, which are common vehicles for mining ventures, and it has no "control" or beneficial-ownership test for foreign-organized affiliates.

12. **Sec. 3(a), territorial reach.** The prohibition covers "any person in the United States" and "any U.S. person anywhere," but "in the United States" is undefined. It does not clarify whether it reaches the Area beyond national jurisdiction, the EEZ, or flag-state waters. Foreign-organized subsidiaries of U.S. companies operating abroad would fall outside the prohibition.

13. **Sec. 3(a), "engage in" is undefined.** The prohibition does not say whether financing, supplying equipment, processing ore, purchasing or shipping nodules, or providing offtake counts as "engaging in" mining. Those activities may stay outside the prohibition.

14. **Sec. 2(3), "covered vessel" and "equipped for."** The 5,000-gross-ton threshold applies only to the registry in Section 4. "Equipped for" is undefined, and the definition does not address support vessels, converted vessels, or vessels that operate collectors from another ship.

**Section 4: Registry and reporting**

15. **Sec. 4(a), no penalty for failing to register.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of Section 3, so a failure to register under Section 4 carries no stated consequence. The duty is also not tied to a deadline.

16. **Sec. 4(b), undefined report contents.** The report must "describe" recovery activities, but the Act does not require tonnage, location, depth, sales, discharge, or environmental data. Reports could be accurate and still say very little.

17. **Sec. 4(b), certification has no standard.** The operator must "certify" the report, but the Act does not say what certification means or attach a false-statement penalty. The only criminal provision in Section 5(b) covers Section 3 violations.

18. **Sec. 4(b), reporting is circular.** Only "registered operators" file reports, and registration is the duty that might not be performed. An unregistered vessel therefore produces no reports, and nothing in the Act requires NOAA to pursue unregistered vessels.

19. **Sec. 4, no public disclosure.** Neither the registry nor the reports are required to be published, which limits public and congressional oversight and makes independent verification harder.

**Section 5: Penalties and enforcement**

20. **Sec. 5(a), per-day cap as cost of doing business.** A maximum of $1 million per day is not tied to tonnage, revenue, or duration, so a profitable operation could treat the penalty as an operating expense. The Act also includes no inflation adjustment and no factors for setting the penalty, such as gravity, duration, good faith, or ability to pay.

21. **Sec. 5(a), "day on which the violation occurs."** The Act does not say whether a continuing operation is one violation or one violation per day, or whether each vessel is a separate violation. The ambiguity makes both the size and the litigation of any penalty uncertain.

22. **Sec. 5(a) vs. Sec. 8, timing mismatch.** Section 5(a) applies to violations "occurring on or after the date of enactment," but Section 3 does not take effect until 180 days later under Section 8. This does not create a violation in the window, but it does give operators a 180-day period to expand operations, file or obtain licenses, and position vessels before the prohibition takes effect.

23. **Sec. 5, no enforcing agency or procedure.** The Act does not designate an agency to bring civil enforcement, specify whether penalties are assessed administratively or in court, or set a limitations period, so the general federal default would apply. Any gap in agency resources or priorities would delay enforcement.

24. **Sec. 5, no equitable or in rem remedies.** The Act does not expressly authorize injunctions, cease-and-desist orders, vessel detention, seizure of equipment or nodules, or forfeiture. Courts may infer some of these, but without express authority, challenges to remedies become a litigation issue.

25. **Sec. 5(b), "willfully" is undefined.** The criminal provision requires willfulness, and an operator who relies in good faith on a grandfathered license or an environmental-assessment label can argue lack of willfulness. The Act does not address officer or organizational liability beyond the general Title 18 fine provisions.

26. **Sec. 5, no citizen suit or whistleblower provision.** Enforcement depends entirely on government action, with no private right to sue and no protection or incentive for insiders who report violations. Enforcement therefore depends on the agency's willingness to act.

**Sections 6–8: International, duration, and effective date**

27. **Sec. 6, obligation to "seek to negotiate."** The Secretary must try to negotiate an agreement within 18 months, but the Act does not require reaching an agreement, report on progress, or link the outcome to the prohibition. "Equivalent" is undefined, so the standard for success is unclear.

28. **Sec. 6 and DSHMRA, no interaction clause.** The Act does not address how it relates to DSHMRA or the ISA framework, and it has no supersession or savings clause. Operators could argue that DSHMRA authorizations, as the more specific statute, survive and that courts should avoid implied repeal.

29. **Sec. 7(a), "serious harm" and "can be conducted" are undefined.** The Act does not define serious harm, does not say whether the test is capability or current practice, and does not say how the finding would be proven or contested. The standard is hard to apply and easy to challenge.

30. **Sec. 7(a), no deadline or mandate for the NASEM report.** The joint-resolution trigger depends on a National Academies report, but the Act does not require NASEM to produce one, set a deadline, or define its scope. Without the report, the finding cannot be made, so the indefinite prohibition may never be lifted, but it also may never be reviewed.

31. **Sec. 7(b), no savings clause.** The Act does not say whether violations occurring before the sunset remain enforceable or whether penalties accrued before the sunset survive. The general federal savings statute (1 U.S.C. § 109) may cover repeals, but its application to a sunset is uncertain.

32. **Sec. 8, transition period with no standstill.** The 180-day delay has no interim requirements such as a standstill, a ban on new licenses, or provisions for vessels in transit or under construction. This gap works in favor of operators who want to expand before the prohibition applies.

33. **Missing implementing authority.** The Act gives no rulemaking authority, no appropriations, no severability clause, and no definition of "vessel" or "operator." Each gap adds time and room for dispute when the Act is implemented.

**Strategic note:** Some of these fixes will be proposed by the sponsors or by opponents of deep-sea mining. Items 1, 6, and 28 are the ones most likely to draw amendments that could tighten the bill in ways that affect us. Advocacy on those points should be sequenced carefully, with the policy team deciding which issues to raise privately and which to raise in the markup.
